cards.title: Start with the Smallest Viable Market, Not the Mass Market
cards.summary: Target a tiny audience who would genuinely miss you before trying to win the mass market.
cards.use_when: Choosing a positioning and target-customer focus for a new store, product line, or niche brand before spending on broad acquisition.
steps: Define the smallest group of buyers you can serve exceptionally, then ask: who would miss this brand if it disappeared? If you cannot win the small group, do not assume you will win the large one.

Follow Kevin Kelly's '1,000 true fans' framing as the source's heuristics for independent creators: roughly a thousand people who will buy nearly everything you release can sustain a living, though not a fortune—treat this as an illustration, not a store benchmark.
Resist 'bending yourself into a pretzel' to please anonymous masses before you have 50–100 people who would miss you.
Build roots in the specific dreams and desires of the niche you serve; a commodity store with shallow roots gets crowded out by similar competitors.
As the niche deepens, its members organically spread the word to the next layer, growing reach without mass-media spend.
caveats: This is the source's argument for connection over hits; it does not claim small markets always beat mass-market plays—the author explicitly says some businesses should chase being the 'hit machine.'
The 1,000-fan figure is a creator-economy heuristic, not a validated ecommerce threshold.

cards.title: Model the Grateful Dead's Small-Market Strategy for Repeat Buyers
cards.summary: The Dead concentrated everything on a tiny devoted audience rather than chasing radio hits—a template for super-fan-centric retail.
cards.use_when: Designing merchandising, drops, loyalty or community programs for a niche brand that wants high repeat purchase rather than broad one-time reach.
steps: Appeal to a relatively small audience and focus all energy on them; skip mass broadcast in favor of fan-to-fan sharing.
Encourage customers to share and even reproduce your content (the Dead encouraged taping) rather than blocking it—hand-to-hand spread replaces paid reach.
Prefer many true fans who support a lot over many casual buyers who support a little.
Own the extremes on a positioning axis (live long jams vs polished records); pick polarizing strengths rather than averaging for everyone.
Give fans something to talk about and stand for, including insider/outsider identity, so community itself drives demand.
caveats: Success required three things the source names explicitly: extraordinary talent, significant patience (it took over a decade; in 1972 only ~5,000 came to a typical show), and the guts to be quirky.

cards.title: Do Not Assume You Can Copy the Hit Machine Model
cards.summary: Hit-maker success exists but is rare; most brands succeed through connection and change rather than mass hits.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pursue mass-market, hit-driven growth or a focused connection strategy for your store.
steps: Recognize that someone will always be the hit machine in a market; the source says it is probably not going to be most brands.
If you genuinely find a playbook to become a hit machine, the author tells you to go for it—there is no law against it.
For most operators, take the alternative path: connection, empathy and change within a chosen group.
Note that even enormous hits now reach tiny fractions of the population (Hamilton seen by under 1% of the U.S.; Mad Men regularly seen by ~1%), so 'hits' are not as total as they once were.
Design your plan around being meaningful to a defined few rather than invisible-but-widely-known.
caveats: The Hamilton and Mad Men figures are the author's illustrative examples, not benchmarks for any store category.

cards.title: Separate Criticism From Useful Advice You Can Act On
cards.summary: Critics describing their feelings are right but not useful; ask for advice framed around how to fit the person's worldview.
cards.use_when: Reviewing negative product reviews, customer feedback, or testing a new PDP/landing-page concept with real shoppers.
steps: Accept that the critic who does not like your work is correct in that they do not like it—arguing is pointless.

Reject the leap that 'no one' will like it; the same product routinely gets one-star and five-star reviews (the source cites 12% of ~21,000 Harry Potter reviews at one or two stars), showing bimodal audiences.
Replace 'what do you think?' feedback requests with advice requests: 'I made something I like and thought you would like; how did it land, and what advice do you have to fit your worldview better?'
Recognize universalizing language ('everyone'/'no one') as a specific sore spot triggered by one moment, not a market signal.
Use the advice to identify fears, dreams and wants of the audience, then adjust product, messaging or merchandising accordingly.
caveats: The Harry Potter review split is an example of bimodal distribution, not evidence your product will be polarizing.

cards.title: Ask Why Non-Buyers Are Right (Empathy Exercise)
cards.summary: Complete the sentence explaining why people who did not buy made a rational choice given what they want and believe.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why an audience segment rejects your store, product or offer, or when repositioning after low conversion.
steps: List the people who do not buy from you, do not take your calls, or buy from a competitor despite knowing you exist.
Suspend the temptation to call them ill-informed, selfish or wrongheaded.
Fill in the sentence: 'For people who want (X) and believe (Y), choosing (your competitor/not buying) is exactly correct.'
Example given: a cooking student asks why ground turkey can replace veal; both teacher and student are right because they care about different things (taste memory vs availability/health/morals).
Use the completed sentence to identify whether the issue is offer, story, price, availability or worldview—then decide whether to serve them or refer them elsewhere.
The source suggests finding freedom by telling mismatched customers: 'this isn't for you, here's my competitor.'
caveats: This is a mindset/empathy exercise; it does not guarantee the segment is winnable—sometimes the correct conclusion is they should buy elsewhere.

cards.title: Use the 'People Like Us Do Things Like This' Frame for Behavior Change
cards.summary: Decisions are driven by fitting one's cohort and status; normalize the new behavior inside the specific group you serve.
cards.use_when: Designing adoption campaigns, community programs or merchandising for a defined tribe (e.g., getting customers to try a new product category).
steps: Recognize the core question buyers ask: 'Do people like me do things like this?'—actions follow cohort perception, not pure rationality (cricket flour vs beef example).
Define 'us' first and specifically; the tighter and more connected the group, the better for change.
Map the worldview of the culture you seek to change, then focus all energy on it and ignore everyone else.
Build and live a story that resonates with that culture, and let core members organically share with the next layer.
Track how normalization creates culture, culture drives choices, and choices reinforce normalization—design your brand into that loop.
caveats: This is a change-thy-culture framework; it will not work on a diffuse mass audience with no shared identity.
The Blue Ribbons case (budget passed 2:1 after ribbons spread town-wide) is a civic example the source uses to illustrate the principle, not a store benchmark.

cards.title: Build an Exclusive Cohort, Not Just an Elite Brand
cards.summary: Exclusive (us vs them) organizations change culture and are controllable; elite status is external and fragile.
cards.use_when: Designing loyalty tiers, member communities, VIP programs or a brand identity based on insider belonging.
steps: Distinguish two measures: elite = external respect (e.g., Rhodes Scholarship); exclusive = an insider tribe (e.g., Hell's Angels). Harvard Business School and Navy SEALs are both.
The source argues exclusive institutions change things and can be controlled; elite status is external and can be taken away instantly.
Build membership so that every member is 'people like us'; signing up gains status and walking away loses it.
Engineer tension and useful connections inside the cohort rather than chasing press validation.
Apply to ecommerce via member-only drops, early access, gated community, or a clear 'in-group' identity—but keep the group meaningfully tight.
caveats: Exclusivity risks alienating the accidental audience; if your model depends on broad reach, weigh this tradeoff.

cards.title: Engineer Peer Pressure Through 'Cash for Status' Mechanics
cards.summary: Robin Hood Foundation's $101M night shows status trading, not the gala format, drives outsized giving.
cards.use_when: Designing high-value fundraising, charitable tie-ins, or VIP purchase experiences tied to social status.
steps: Identify the cohort where relative status is deeply felt (the source cites hypercompetitive Wall Street investors for Robin Hood).
Build a visible, time-bound event or drop where peers and spouses are present so that status competition activates.
Offer a simple trade: cash for status. Auctions or limited purchases let buyers raise profile and 'win' against peers.
Spread word about early adopters' generosity over years to normalize the expectation.
Repeat so the behavior becomes 'what we do,' not an extreme act—the tension becomes the norm over time.
caveats: The $101M figure is a single historical outcome the source uses as illustration, not a promise.
The source stresses this is intentional and rarely an accidental side effect; venue/format alone does not produce it.

cards.title: Plan for Pattern Match vs Pattern Interrupt
cards.summary: Fitting an existing buying pattern is easy; breaking one requires tension—target buyers whose patterns are not yet set.
cards.use_when: Deciding go-to-market approach for a new product category, new store, or a subscription that replaces an incumbent habit.
steps: Classify your offer: does it slot into an existing routine (pattern match) or replace an established habit (pattern interrupt)?
If pattern match, simply place your product into the existing cadence—cheap and low-friction.
If pattern interrupt, accept that most recipients will say no; you must first undo the old pattern before earning forward motion.

Prioritize people whose life context already broke their pattern: new dads, engaged couples, people who recently moved (the source calls these segments highly profitable because there is no pattern to match).
For apps or platforms, market when the underlying platform habit is new, so you do not have to convince buyers their old choices were mistakes.
caveats: Buying managers in organizations are trained to match patterns for job security; do not assume you can interrupt a procurement habit without strong justification.

cards.title: Create Tension to Move Customers Forward (Not Fear)
cards.summary: Tension—the pull of being left behind or missing out—removes inertia; fear paralyzes instead.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition or cart-recovery messaging for an offer that requires breaking an existing habit or decision.
steps: Identify the specific tension your offer can create: what becomes less true for the buyer if they don't act?

Examples from the source: scarcity of a going-out-of-business sale; early adopter benefit on a new social app; last three houses on your block sold below expectations; Supreme making only 250 units; TV series finale this Sunday.
Apply the slack analogy: using the product is better when peers use it, giving existing users a selfish reason to invite others; a colleague saying 'you're missing out' is the pattern interrupt.
Make the tension resolvable by a single, simple forward action—sign in, buy, sign up.
Explicitly test whether the message creates tension or fear; if it coerces or scares, the source says you are probably doing it wrong.
caveats: Tension works because of status and cohort belonging; it is not the same as fear, and should not be used manipulatively.
The examples (Slack, Supreme, casinos) are illustrations; do not assume the same tension will move your specific audience.

cards.title: Decide Whether Your Store Is a Cab or an Agent of Change
cards.summary: Two paths: ride on demand as a replaceable cog, or create tension and then relieve it with your offer.
cards.use_when: Setting brand strategy and differentiating from commoditized competitors in your category.
steps: Ask honestly which you are: a cab driver who shows up and charges the meter, or an agent of change who creates tension and then relieves it.
If cab: compete on execution and price; not much else changes no matter how hard you work.
If agent of change: identify what your launch makes no longer true (e.g., the second hotel makes the first no longer 'the only one'; the telephone makes the telegraph no longer fastest).
Aim for extremes (most efficient, least expensive, most convenient) so whatever you exceed is no longer the extreme its fans sought.
When a new network or brand gains the cool kids, existing alternatives lose traction—use this to plan entry timing and partnerships.
caveats: This is the source's framing of two marketing postures, not a claim that one is always correct; some markets simply need another good option.

cards.title: Remember the Status Quo Resists You Because of Status, Not Truth
cards.summary: The dominant narrative survives because of cultural status dynamics, not for lack of a better idea.
cards.use_when: Planning competitive entry against a market leader or legacy category belief.
steps: Accept that the market leader, policies and procedures exist for a reason and are good at resisting insurgents.
Stop assuming a better idea, simpler solution or more efficient procedure is enough—the source says if that were true we would have changed long ago.
Focus on shifting the culture of a specific group rather than winning an argument on merits.
Remember the engine of culture is status; frame your offer in terms of how the buyer's status shifts (up, or safely down).
Use the 'us vs them' exclusive group to accumulate cultural momentum rather than fighting the incumbent head-on.
caveats: This is a strategic posture; it does not mean product quality is irrelevant, only that correctness alone is insufficient.

cards.title: View Every Purchase Through Status Roles
cards.summary: Status is relative, perceived, learned, inertial, and shame can destabilize it—use it as a lens on purchase decisions.
cards.use_when: Designing product tiers, brand imagery, influencer partnerships, or loyalty perks where buyers signal who they are.
steps: Use the six properties from the source: status is relative (no absolute scale); it is in the eye of the beholder; only status attended to matters; it has inertia (people defend their role); it is learned; shame is the status killer.

Map your customer's external status (how their community sees them) and internal status (how they see themselves), then infer behavior patterns: belittling others, seeking approval, selfless help, striving for more.
Note that not everyone wants higher status—some fight to stay or even move lower (coal miner example); designing for upward movement only can miss segments.
Consider that status is not wealth: a local yogi may outrank the richest man in town with certain peers.
Apply to product tiers, premium imagery, or memberships as signals buyers can use to reinforce or shift their standing.
caveats: The source warns that using status in marketing is walking on thin ice; you cannot know whether an outwardly high-status customer actually believes it or wants more.

cards.title: Adapt Ritual and Status Instead of Fighting Cultural Beliefs
cards.summary: Lion Guardians changed a Maasai rite of passage from killing lions to saving them by honoring underlying desires.
cards.use_when: Adapting a brand, product or category to sensitive cultural or identity-driven customer behaviors.
steps: Identify the underlying human desires your audience's behavior serves (binding community, empowerment, bravery, patience, rite of passage) rather than attacking the surface behavior.
Recognize that killing a lion was historically tied to status for Maasai youth—rational arguments alone could not shift the belief.
Work within the cultural system to introduce a new behavior that satisfies the same desires and confers equivalent status.
For ecommerce: when a behavior (e.g., ritual consumption, gifting) serves identity, design products and messaging that honor the identity rather than asking customers to abandon it.
Anchor new behaviors to existing rituals and social proof so adoption feels like belonging, not breaking from the group.
caveats: This case involves community-level conservation work by Leela Hazzah's team; do not transpose numeric wildlife estimates to product strategy.
Cultural sensitivity is required; outsider framing that ignores underlying desires will fail.

cards.title: Segment by Affiliation vs Dominion Worldview
cards.summary: Some buyers measure status by who trusts them; others by who has power—design messages for the metric they use.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition creative, influencer briefs or loyalty messaging for distinct buyer segments.
steps: Diagnose which worldview your segment holds. Affiliation questions: who knows you, who trusts you, have you made things better, what's your circle, where do you stand within the tribe?
Dominion questions: this is mine not yours, who has more power, I did this myself, my family needs more, my side dominating yours.
Match language: affiliation audiences respond to community, sync, and mutual support (e.g., jazz band keeping in sync); dominion audiences respond to competitive wins and dominance.
Recognize that a person can hold different frames in different contexts (the same 12-year-old cares about winning on the field but who sits next to them on the bus).
Use the distinction to segment creative and offers rather than averaging messaging to total blandness.
caveats: Affiliation and dominion are worldviews the source presents as analytical lenses; they are not strictly binary and can shift with context.

cards.title: Engineer a Standing Ovation: Seed a Small Number of Status Leaders
cards.summary: A few respected insiders can trigger a cascade of public adoption, but only where trust and belonging are strong.
cards.use_when: Planning product launches, review/social-proof seeding, or community engagement campaigns.
steps: Identify how many respected insiders are needed to trigger cascading adoption in your venue; the source's illustration claims as few as three at TED and roughly fifteen strangers spread through a Broadway theater.
Recognize that in rooms with trust and recognition among attendees, few strangers are needed because people want to align with respected leaders.
In venues of strangers or with strong anti-standing-ovation norms (e.g., Mezzrow jazz club), cascades may be nearly impossible regardless of effort.
Apply to launches: seed a small, visible group of respected customers whose behavior others will mirror, especially in high-trust communities.
Use the venue's existing bias as a constraint—if the culture rejects the behavior, plan to change the venue or segment instead.
caveats: The number thresholds (three, fifteen) are illustrative of the mechanism, not universal rules; audience composition matters more than headcount.

cards.title: Define the 'Us' Explicitly in Marketing Statements
cards.summary: When saying 'people like us do things like this,' a specific 'us' is required—otherwise the statement means nothing.
cards.use_when: Writing brand manifestos, community guidelines, or acquisition copy that invokes an in-group.
steps: Replace universal audiences ('Americans,' 'everyone') with a tightly defined 'us' that actually exists.
Avoid the backwards formulation 'the people who give are people like us'; instead specify the identity, values and behaviors that define the group.
Map the worldview of that culture and focus all energy there, ignoring everyone else as the source directs.
Use the group's shared behaviors as proof points ('people like us own a car; we don't take the bus') to make the offer feel like belonging.
Apply the same logic internally—pitch ideas to a defined 'us' in meetings, not a universal crowd.
caveats: The tighter the us, the more effective for change, but the smaller the addressable market; balance reach against relevance deliberately.

cards.title: Use the Roots and Shoots Metaphor to Plan Brand Growth
cards.summary: Deep roots in a niche's dreams and desires let the brand grow into a beacon that crowds out commodity competitors.
cards.use_when: Planning long-term brand differentiation and category dominance instead of rapid commodity launches.
steps: Plant roots in the soil of the dreams and desires of the specific people you seek to serve—not everyone.
Avoid shallow 'quick response to obvious demand' positioning, which produces a commodity that gets crowded out.
Grow the tree: early adopters engage, climb, use shade, eat fruit, and attract others.
Exploit the open canopy—if few similar trees exist, grow taller faster and become the dominant choice in the neighborhood.
Remember the market likes a winner; once dominant, the tree's height blocks futile efforts of similar competitors.
Do not expect a crowd from an acorn—work that matters for people who care is the shortest route to impact.
caveats: Metaphor is strategic framing (the author's), not an operational model with timelines or metrics.

cards.title: Position Just Ahead of Today—But Not Too Far
cards.summary: Meaningful change sits one step ahead of current culture; leap too far and the tribe will not follow.
cards.use_when: Designing product aesthetics, campaign concepts or brand refresh that must read as fresh but still familiar.
steps: Study the hierarchy of yesterday, today and tomorrow in your category; you cannot jump straight to tomorrow.
Imitate yesterday's style is technically easy but offers no differentiation; aim to establish the next phase with something 'a bit better and a bit unexpected.'
Use the JetBlue/Virgin America illustration: JetBlue only had to be hipper than American and Delta; Virgin America had to be hipper than JetBlue—each launch faced a raised bar.
Calibrate the leap by asking whether the tribe will follow; if too far, you lose them.
Apply to ecommerce brand design, packaging and creative—being one step ahead is differentiating; being ten steps ahead is alienating.
caveats: The JetBlue/Virgin comparison is the source's illustration; the 'how far is too far' threshold is contextual.

cards.title: Build a Peer-Powered Ratchet Like Slack
cards.summary: Products used together by teams gain a selfish reason for existing users to convert coworkers—driving viral pattern interrupts.
cards.use_when: Designing referral mechanics, collaboration features, subscription plans for teams, or buyer-side network effects.
steps: Identify whether your product is better when peers or teammates use it. If yes, existing users have a powerful selfish reason to recruit.
Reduce the friction for the peer-to-peer pattern interrupt: a colleague's simple statement 'we're going to try this new tool' should be enough.
Provide that message as part of the product itself (sharing invites, collaborative workspaces, joint accounts) so the horizontal transmission is built in.
Sequence go-to-market: first pattern match early adopters who love new tools; then let them trigger the pattern interrupt for their colleagues.
Give existing users a felt cost of delay ('you're missing out; people at work are talking without you') to accelerate the ratchet.
caveats: Slack is the source's example; network-effect design does not automatically produce virality, and the mechanics depend on the product category.

cards.title: Interpret Famous Cases Without Copying Tactics Blindly
cards.summary: The tactic in a famous success (gala, format, campaign) is rarely the actual secret—the peer pressure and context is.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to replicate a well-known competitor's marketing format or campaign structure.
steps: When a tactic looks like the cause of a hit, ask what underlying mechanism actually drove results.
Use Robin Hood Foundation as the example: many concluded the gala format raised $101M; the source argues it was peer pressure, status trading and decades of normalization.
Look for the cohort dynamics, historical context and status economics that a copycat would also have to recreate.
Recognize that intentional, long-cultivated processes (spreading word about early adopters, building competitive tension) usually underpin outcomes, not a single night's format.
Before copying a famous tactic, inventory whether you have the audience, history and status dynamics it depends on.
caveats: The $101M figure and Robin Hood context are examples of the source's analytical argument; do not treat them as reproducible benchmarks.

A thousand true fans In 2008 Kevin Kelly, founding editor of Wired, wrote an essay that described the simple truth of the smallest viable market. For the independent creator of intellectual property (a singer, perhaps, or a writer), it turns out that a thousand true fans might be sufficient to live a betterthan-decent life. To quote Kevin, “A true fan is defined as a fan that will buy anything you produce. These diehard fans will drive two hundred miles to see you sing; they will buy the hardback and paperback and Audible versions of your book; they will purchase your next figurine sight unseen; they will pay for the ‘best-of’ DVD version of your free YouTube channel; they will come to your chef’s table once a month. If you have roughly a thousand true fans like this (also known as super fans), you can make a living—if you are content to make a living but not a fortune.” That’s one thousand people who will support you on Patreon, or one thousand people who will buy your new project on Kickstarter the day you launch it.

 It’s one thousand people who not only care about your work but also spread the word to those around them. The challenge for most people who seek to make an impact isn’t winning over the mass market. It’s the micro market. They bend themselves into a pretzel trying to please the anonymous masses before they have fifty or one hundred people who would miss them if they were gone. While it might be comforting to dream of becoming a Kardashian, it’s way While it might be comforting to dream of becoming a Kardashian, it’s way more productive to matter to a few instead. But what about Hamilton? The hit that proves the theory. The hit that represents not only the triumph of one creator over the status quo, but the magical narrative of a singular piece of effort and art that changes everything. Except. Except, for more than a year, Hamilton was seen by only a few hundred people a night. Except that even when it is running at full capacity in New York, breaking records on Broadway, it’s only being seen by a few thousand people. Except that even as it’s changing a small part of the culture in cities like Chicago, it has been seen by less than 1 percent of the U.S. population. Its bestselling soundtrack album only sold a few hundred thousand copies. And the companion book, a surprise bestseller, sold about that many as well. Our hits aren’t hits anymore, not like they used to be. Instead, they are meaningful for a few and invisible to the rest. What would Jerry do? I often tell the story of the Grateful Dead, and yet almost no one has the guts to commit to this sort of service, the leadership of connection. I first wrote about them ten years ago, and yet too many of us fall into the trap of seeking whatever passes for the Top 40 in our industry instead. So far I’ve purchased 233 different Grateful Dead albums, more than five hundred hours of music altogether. The Dead are an almost perfect example of the power of marketing for the smallest viable market. It’s worth a few minutes to deconstruct what they did and how they did it, because it will inform the long, strange trip we’re on here. Although it’s become a familiar example, musicians, publishers, gym owners, consultants, chefs, and teachers seem to forget the core lesson in the Dead’s failure to race for a hit. First, few kids grow up wanting to start a band like the Grateful Dead. The Dead had a grand total of one top 40 Billboard hit. One. They’re easily dismissed as some sort of quirky hippie band. They have fans, true fans, fans who are also easily dismissed as quirky hippies. true fans, fans who are also easily dismissed as quirky hippies. And yet . . . And yet the Dead grossed more than $350 million in revenue while Jerry Garcia was alive, and another $100 million since his death. I’m not even counting record sales, just concert tickets. Most of that run was accomplished when ticket prices averaged just twenty-three dollars. How? Because the true fans showed up. Because the true fans spread the word. And because the true fans never fully satisfied their need to be connected. Here are the key elements of the Dead’s marketing success: They appealed to a relatively tiny audience and focused all their energy on them. They didn’t use radio to spread their ideas to the masses. Instead, they relied on fans to share the word, hand to hand, by encouraging them to tape their shows. Instead of hoping to encourage a large number of people to support them a little, they relied on a small number of true fans who supported them a lot. They picked the extremes on the XY axis (live concerts vs. polished records, long jams for the fan family vs. short hits for the radio) and owned them both. They gave the fans plenty to talk about and stand for. Insiders and outsiders. They needed three things to pull this off: Extraordinary talent. You can’t fake your way through 146 concerts in a year. Significant patience. In 1972, considered by some to be a peak year for the band, only five thousand people came to a typical show. It took more than a decade before the Dead became an “overnight” success. The guts to be quirky. It couldn’t have been easy to watch the Zombies, the Doors, and even the Turtles sell far more records than they did. For a while, anyway. In 1972, being obstinate, generous, and lucky was an accident that led to their surprising success. Today, though, in most industries (including the music business) this sort of success is not an accident. It’s the best path to success, and in many ways, the most rewarding as well. Taylor Swift is not your role model Consider Scott Borchetta, who runs Big Machine records. He’s had more than two hundred number-one singles. That’s an awe-inspiring total. A world-class marketer. He’s sold more than thirty million records for Taylor Swift, and Swift’s tour revenue is about the same as the Dead’s was. Taylor and Scott are hit machines. Most markets need someone to be a hit machine, and for the music business right now, it’s them. As we’ll see, every long tail has a short head, a place where the hits live. Hits serve a useful purpose to our culture, but the essential lesson is this: someone is going to make hits, and it’s probably not going to be you. If you can find a playbook on how to become a hit machine, to become the one who regularly creates the mass movement that changes the middle of the market, go for it! For the rest of us, there’s the other path: the path of connection, empathy, and change. All critics are right (all critics are wrong) The critic who doesn’t like your work is correct. He doesn’t like your work. This cannot be argued with. The critic who says that no one else will like your work is wrong. After all, you like your work. Someone else might like it too. This is the only way to understand the one-star and five-star reviews that every bestselling book on Amazon receives. How could one book possibly get both? Either it’s good or it’s not. Not true. Twelve percent of the twenty-one thousand reviews for Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone gave it one or two stars. To visualize that: out of one hundred readers, twelve said it was one of the worst books they’d ever read. What this bimodal distribution teaches us is that there are at least two audiences that interact with every bestselling book. There’s the desired audience, the one that has a set of dreams and beliefs and wants that perfectly integrates with this work. And there’s the accidental audience, the one that gets more satisfaction out of not liking the work, out of hating it, and sharing that thought with others. They’re both right. But neither is particularly useful. When we seek feedback, we’re doing something brave and foolish. We’re asking to be proven wrong. To have people say “You thought you made something great, but you didn’t.” Ouch. What if, instead, we seek advice? Seek it like this: “I made something that I like, that I thought you’d like. How’d I do? What advice do you have for how I could make it fit your worldview more closely?” That’s not criticism. Or feedback. That sort of helpful advice reveals a lot about the person you’re engaging with. It helps us see his or her fears and dreams and wants. It’s a clue on how to get even closer next time. Plenty of people can tell you how your work makes them feel. We’re intimately familiar with the noise in our own heads, and that noise is often expressed as personal and specific criticism. But it might not be about you and it might not be useful. Perhaps you’re hearing about someone’s fears, or their narrative about inadequacy or unfairness. When people share their negative stories, they often try to broaden the response and universalize it. They talk about how “no one” or “everyone” will feel. But what you’re actually hearing about is a specific sore spot that was touched in a specific moment by a specific piece of work. This is the person who posts a one-star review because the book arrived late for the baby shower. Or the customer who’s angry because she spent more than she budgeted for on her wedding. That’s quite different from someone giving you useful advice about how to work with someone like them in the future. It’s worth the effort to insulate ourselves from a raw emotional onslaught and to tease out substantial useful direction instead. to tease out substantial useful direction instead. Why don’t people choose you? Here’s another difficult exercise, one that stretches the empathy muscle of a typical marketer: Those people who don’t buy from you, the ones who don’t take your calls, who sneer at your innovations, who happily buy from a competitor even if they know you exist . . . those people . . . Why are they right? Why are the people who don’t choose you correct in their decision to not choose you? If you’ve worked hard, it’s tempting to denigrate their judgment, to question their values, and assume that these folks are either ill-informed, selfish, or simply wrongheaded. Put that aside for a moment and find the empathy to fill in this sentence: “For people who want what you want (____) and believe what you believe (____), your choice of ____ is exactly correct.” Because it is. People are quite likely to make perfectly rational decisions based on what they see, what they believe, and what they want. If you’re a career coach, then explain why people who don’t hire a coach have made a smart decision. Or explain why people who are using someone else to coach them have done something that makes sense for them. Years ago, I went to a cooking class that a friend had bought me as a gift. The chef was teaching everyone to make a dish that used ground veal. “Any questions?” he asked. One student had the temerity to raise his hand and ask, “Is it okay to make this dish with ground turkey instead?” In a thick accent, the chef sneered, “You could . . . if you wanted it to taste like dirt.” Of course, they were both right. For the student, the availability, health benefits, or moral imperatives associated with choosing turkey over veal might mean that he cared more about the story than he did about matching the taste profile that was on offer. For the teacher, for whom the Proustian memory of this dish was everything, the idea of substitutions disrespected the effort he was putting into his work. That’s what right means in this case. Based on who they are and what they want and what they know, everyone is right. Every time. When we find the empathy to say, “I’m sorry, this isn’t for you, here’s the phone number of my competitor,” then we also find the freedom to do work that matters. CHAPTER NINE People Like Us Do Things Like This Deep change is difficult, and worth it As we’ve seen, every organization, every project, every interaction exists to do one thing: to make change happen. To make a sale, to change a policy, to heal the world. As marketers and agents of change, we almost always overrate our ability to make change happen. The reason is simple. In the last few decades, we’ve gotten lazier in our nuance of awarding status, preferring it to be related to either the dollars in a bank account or the number of followers online. But status continues to take many forms. Six things about status 1. Status is always relative. Unlike eyesight or strength or your bank balance, it doesn’t matter where you are on the absolute scale. Instead, it’s about perception of status relative to others in the group. 6 is bigger than 4, but lower than 11. There is no highest number. 2. Status is in the eyes of the beholder. If you are seen as low status by outsiders but as high status in your own narrative, then both things are true, at different times, to different people. 3. Status attended to is the status that matters. Status is most relevant when we try to keep it or change it. For many people, status is upmost in our minds in every interaction. But it only matters when the person we’re engaging with cares about status. 4. Status has inertia. We’re more likely to work to maintain our status (high or low) than we are to try to change it. 5. Status is learned. Our beliefs about status start early. And yet the cohort we are with can influence our perception of our status in very little time. 6. Shame is the status killer. The reason that shame is used as a lever is simple: it works. If we accept the shame someone sends our way, it undermines our entire narrative about relative status. Learning to see status The idea of status isn’t nearly as simple as it appears. Consider, for those you seek to serve, their external status (how they are seen by their chosen community) and their internal status (who they see when they look in the mirror). Next, work through how they maintain or seek to change that status. Do they belittle others? Seek approval? Help in selfless ways? Drive themselves to achieve more? What sort of wins and losses do they track? Consider the following two XY grids. People in the top-right quadrant (a) are rare indeed. This space belongs to people who are seen as powerful and who also see themselves as able to handle it. I’d put Oprah Winfrey in this category. This is the person who is able to choose, not the one who is waiting to be chosen. The top-left quadrant (d) is more common, since people who end up with high status often doubt themselves. This can turn them into divas. The best stories about Frank Sinatra are about the juxtaposition of his perceived royalty status with his own need for affirmation. Impostor syndrome lies here. The bottom-right quadrant (b) is for people who see themselves as far better than the rest of the world does. This is where you can find artistic drive and a willingness to strive for better. Different stories for different people We each have our own narratives. The noise in our head, the worldview that is unique to us, the history and beliefs and perceptions that shape who we are and what we choose. And sonder is the generous act of accepting that others don’t want, believe, or know what we do—and have a similar noise in their heads. But in order to bring our change to the world, we need to make some assumptions about what others believe. We can’t hear the noise in their heads, but we can watch what they do and make some guesses. There is a schism in our culture. In various moments, there are two sides that tell themselves very different stories and act them out in different ways: 1) the populations that default, in certain settings, to dominion, and 2) those that seek affiliation. Affiliation and dominion are different ways to measure status Every search on “nicest guy in Hollywood” brings up a picture of Tom Hanks. And every search on “The Godfather” brings us a picture of the fictional Don Corleone. Tom Hanks cares about affiliation. Don Corleone measured domination instead. Seeing the difference unlocks an understanding of our world, our political landscape, and how your customers might see things. This section of our journey is filled with personas, narratives, and exaggerations about each worldview. Affiliation: The questions that someone who cares about affiliation asks himself and those around him: Who knows you? Who trusts you? Have you made things better? Have you made things better? What is your circle like? Where do you stand within the tribe? Can’t we all get along? Dominion: The questions and statements that someone who cares about dominion offers to himself and those around him: This is mine, not yours. Who has more power? I did this myself. My family needs more of what we already have. My side dominating your side means I don’t have to be in charge, as long as my leader is winning. On the ball field, a twelve-year-old might care about nothing but winning. And not just winning, but beating the opposition. He’ll impugn the referee’s motives, stomp on toes, and hold nothing back in order to win. That same kid doesn’t care at all about being at the top of his class, but he cares a lot about who sits next to him on the bus. In the jazz band, someone is keeping track of how many solos he gets, and someone else wants to be sure she’s helping keep the group in sync. The people you’re seeking to serve in this moment: What are they measuring? If you want to market to someone who measures dominion or affiliation, you’ll need to be aware of what’s being measured and why. “Who eats first” and “who sits closest to the emperor” are questions that persist to this day. Both are status questions. One involves dominion; the other involves affiliation. Not simply eating first, but being on the same team as the person who eats first. And getting pleasure out of watching others eat last. Not simply sitting near the emperor, but knowing that you’ll be in his good graces (and those of the rest of the royal court) tomorrow as well. Which is the narrative your audience resonates with? Learning from pro wrestling What is pro wrestling, really, but a battle for status? It’s not just among the wrestlers, but also among the fans. Because when your hero moves up, so do you. If you can see the lens that pro wrestling and its fans use to see the world while they’re at a match, you can understand how some people will view your offering as well. The alternative to dominion is affiliation One can gain status without an oil well or a factory. And one can enjoy as much status by letting someone into the flow of traffic as they can from cutting him off.
